methods.label: Compare the three digit-column sums
methods.explanation:
The wraparound condition makes the three digit columns contain the same digits with the same multiplicities. To see this, match each term with its successor, taking the first term as the successor of the last. Every tens digit becomes the successor's hundreds digit, and every units digit becomes the successor's tens digit. Since every term position has exactly one successor, these matches merely reorder the entries, even if some terms repeat.

Let \(H\) be the sum of the hundreds digits. The tens digits and the units digits also each sum to \(H\). Adding the terms by place value therefore gives
\[
S=100H+10H+H=111H=3\cdot37H.
\]
Thus the prime \(37\) divides every possible \(S\).

We must also rule out a larger prime that might always divide the sum. The sequence \(123,231,312\) satisfies every digit-matching rule, including the last-to-first rule, and its sum is
\[
123+231+312=666=2\cdot3^2\cdot37.
\]
This admissible sum has no prime factor larger than \(37\), so no larger prime can divide all admissible sums. The largest prime that always divides \(S\) is \(\boxed{37}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
